newsitem.title: USA: Chip industry book-to-bill seen up at 0.94 or 0.95.
newsitem.headline: Chip industry book-to-bill seen up at 0.94 or 0.95.

text.p: The semiconductor industry, buoyed by a rebound in demand, is expected to report Tuesday that a key measure of industry health rose to the highest level of the year in September, analysts said Monday.

The U.S. Semiconductor Industry Association is expected to report in its so-called book-to-bill ratio that the industry received about $95 worth of new orders for every $100 worth of chips it sold in September, analysts said.

The is a leading indicator of future demand, measuring new orders against sales in a month. At 0.95, the ratio would be higher than it has been all year, bringing it close to a break-even point of 1.0.
"It will show sequential improvement," said Mark Edelstone of Prudential Securities, adding it could be surprisingly good.

Analysts are optimistic because personal computer makers such as Intel Corp. have sharply increased their orders for microprocessors and other chips built into personal computers, and are preparing for their biggest selling season, autumn.

Moreover, Dynamic Random Access Memory (DRAM) chip prices finally ended their eight-month slide in mid-September, analysts said. Since memory chips make up about 40 percent of the unit volume of semiconductors shipped in a year, their prices have had a big influence on orders and sales measured in dollars.
"It (the ratio) will be driven by PC demand and DRAM price improvements," said Dan Niles of Robertson, Stephens & Co., who forecast a ratio of 0.98.
PaineWebber Inc. analyst John Lazlo, who expects a 0.95 reading, attributed the expected improvement mostly to personal computer manufacturers' orders.

Edelstone sees a good chance that the September ratio will top most estimates because of the rebound in memory chip prices, which are a fraction of their January levels. "Most of this year, DRAMs have been pressuring the ratio," he said.
But since mid-September, memory prices have risen 30 percent to 50 percent from their lows, Edelstone said. That gain could show up in either the September or October book-to-bill ratio.
Micron Technology Inc., the leading U.S. maker of memory chips, said late last week that memory chip inventories are down to desirable levels from formerly excessive levels.
